title: Brain and Spinal Cord Structures
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter maps the major structures of the brain and spinal cord to what they do: the primary and language cortices, the basal ganglia loops, the cerebellum, the thalamic relay nuclei, the levels of the brainstem and spinal cord, and the systems that keep us conscious. Board questions are usually localization puzzles. They describe a deficit and ask for the lesion, or name a lesion and ask for the deficit and its side. If you know what each structure normally contributes, which pathways cross, and where they cross, you can work out the answer instead of memorizing lists.
prerequisites: Neural tube derivatives and the divisions of the brain (NE-1)
Neurons, glia, and excitatory versus inhibitory synapses (NE-2, NE-13)
Major ascending sensory and descending motor tracts and their decussations (NE-5, NE-7)
G protein signaling through Gs and Gi and cAMP

connections.to: Cerebral blood supply and stroke (NE-10, NE-20-A)
connections.how: Arterial territories decide which cortical, thalamic, or brainstem structures a stroke removes, so vascular syndromes are tested through the localization taught here.
Parkinson and Huntington disease are explained by the basal ganglia circuit, and their pathology (Lewy bodies, CAG expansion) explains which neurons die.
The brainstem level of each cranial nerve nucleus and the position of the conus and cauda equina underlie cranial nerve and root syndromes.

connections.to: Raised intracranial pressure and herniation (NE-4, NE-20-C)
connections.how: Herniation causes coma by compressing the upper brainstem arousal system described in the last section.
The association cortex builds on the primary areas and language areas introduced here.

terms.def: The orderly mapping of body regions onto a strip of cortex or a nucleus, so that neighboring body parts are represented by neighboring neurons.
Loss of the same half of the visual field (right or left) in both eyes, caused by a lesion behind the optic chiasm.
An acquired disorder of language (producing or understanding words), as distinct from dysarthria, which is a disorder of articulation.
Excitation of a target produced by inhibiting the neurons that normally inhibit it.
The GABAergic projection neuron of the striatum, which forms both the direct and the indirect basal ganglia pathways.
Loss of coordination of voluntary movement, with errors of direction, range, force, and timing, in the absence of weakness.
Inability to perform rapidly alternating movements, such as pronation and supination of the hand, smoothly and rhythmically.
Tremor that is absent at rest and grows as a limb approaches a target, typical of cerebellar hemisphere disease.
A thalamic nucleus that receives one type of input and projects it to one specific cortical area.
The tapered lower end of the spinal cord, lying near the L1 to L2 vertebral level in adults.
Neurons of the upper pontine and midbrain tegmentum that project through the thalamus, hypothalamus, and basal forebrain to keep the cortex aroused.
Irreversible loss of all function of the entire brain, including the brainstem, with coma, absent brainstem reflexes, and apnea.

sections.title: Primary cortical areas, language areas, and the deficits their lesions produce

blocks.text: Each primary cortical area handles one kind of information and is laid out as a map. The primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4) occupies the precentral gyrus and the front of the paracentral lobule; its layer V pyramidal neurons, including the giant Betz cells, contribute heavily to the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts. The primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, and 2) lies just behind it in the postcentral gyrus and receives touch, position, pain, and temperature relayed from the opposite side through the thalamus. Both strips follow the same somatotopy: the leg and foot sit on the medial surface, while the trunk, arm, hand, and face run down the lateral convexity, with the hand and face given the most cortex because they need the finest control.

Because the motor and sensory pathways cross, lesions of either strip give contralateral signs, and the arterial territory predicts which part of the body is affected. Anterior cerebral artery occlusion damages the medial strip and weakens the leg more than the arm; middle cerebral artery occlusion damages the lateral strip and affects the face and arm more than the leg. A motor cortex lesion is an upper motor neuron lesion, with weakness that is flaccid at first and later spastic, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response. Facial weakness spares the forehead, because the upper facial motor neurons receive input from both hemispheres. A somatosensory cortex lesion mainly removes discriminative sensation, such as position sense, two-point discrimination, and stereognosis, while crude pain and temperature awareness is relatively spared because it can reach consciousness at the thalamic level.

The primary visual cortex lines the calcarine sulcus. Each side receives the opposite visual field from both eyes, so a lesion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Posterior cerebral artery infarcts often spare central vision, because the occipital pole, where the macula is represented, frequently receives collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery. The primary auditory cortex sits on the transverse temporal gyri. Above the cochlear nuclei auditory pathways project to both sides, so a one-sided lesion barely reduces hearing and mainly impairs sound localization.

Language is lateralized to the dominant hemisphere, the left in nearly all right-handed and most left-handed people. Broca area assembles the motor program for speech, so its loss leaves comprehension intact but speech effortful, sparse, and telegraphic, and patients are aware of their errors. Wernicke area links speech sounds to meaning, so its loss leaves speech fluent but full of wrong and invented words, comprehension poor, and the patient often unaware. Both impair repetition, because each area is part of the repetition loop that the arcuate fasciculus connects.

Contralateral loss of position sense, fine touch, stereognosis
Banks of the calcarine sulcus, occipital lobe
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often macular sparing

sections.title: Direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways, Parkinson disease, and Huntington disease

blocks.text: The basal ganglia send no fibers to the spinal cord; they adjust movement through a loop that runs from cortex to striatum to globus pallidus to thalamus and back to cortex. The key to the circuit is its output: the internal globus pallidus (GPi), together with the substantia nigra pars reticulata, fires tonically and releases GABA onto the ventral anterior and ventral lateral (VA and VL) thalamus. The motor thalamus is therefore held under a constant brake. Movement is allowed by releasing that brake selectively.

The striatum (caudate and putamen) receives glutamate from the cortex. Its GABAergic medium spiny neurons form two pathways. Direct pathway neurons carry D1 receptors and project to the GPi. Indirect pathway neurons carry D2 receptors and project to the external globus pallidus (GPe), which normally inhibits the subthalamic nucleus; the subthalamic nucleus in turn excites the GPi with glutamate. Counting inhibitory links gives the net effect: two in the direct route excite the thalamus, three in the indirect route inhibit it.

blocks.title: Direct pathway (go)
steps: Cortex excites D1 striatal neurons (glutamate)
Striatum inhibits GPi (GABA)
GPi releases its inhibition of VA and VL thalamus
Thalamus excites motor cortex
Movement is facilitated
blocks.caption: Two inhibitory links in series produce net excitation of the thalamus.

blocks.title: Indirect pathway (stop)
steps: Cortex excites D2 striatal neurons (glutamate)
Striatum inhibits GPe (GABA)
Subthalamic nucleus is released from GPe inhibition
Subthalamic nucleus excites GPi (glutamate)
GPi inhibits VA and VL thalamus more strongly
Movement is suppressed
blocks.caption: Three inhibitory links plus one excitatory link produce net inhibition of the thalamus.

blocks.text: Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) acts on both pathways. Through D1 receptors (Gs) it makes direct pathway neurons more responsive to cortex; through D2 receptors (Gi) it makes indirect pathway neurons less responsive. Both effects favor movement, which is why D2 receptor blockers produce parkinsonism.

In Parkinson disease, pigmented SNc neurons degenerate, with Lewy bodies containing alpha-synuclein, and signs appear only after most nigrostriatal neurons are lost. The motor thalamus is overinhibited (see the worked example), producing bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability, a masked face, and a shuffling gait. Huntington disease is autosomal dominant, caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, and shows anticipation. Its polyglutamine protein kills striatal medium spiny neurons, and the indirect pathway neurons projecting to the GPe are lost first, so the GPi brake weakens and chorea appears. Caudate atrophy enlarges the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles; later loss of direct pathway neurons adds rigidity, while damage to caudate and prefrontal loops explains the dementia and psychiatric change. A small infarct of the subthalamic nucleus removes its drive to the GPi and produces contralateral hemiballismus.

blocks.title: Basal ganglia disorders by mechanism
rows: Too little movement: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor
Loss of indirect pathway striatal neurons, caudate first
Violent flinging of the contralateral limbs
blocks.caption: Hypokinetic disorders raise GPi output; hyperkinetic disorders lower it.

blocks.title: Worked example: predicting the signs of dopamine loss
blocks.text: Direct pathway: D1 excitation falls, striatal inhibition of the GPi falls, and GPi output rises. Indirect pathway: D2 inhibition is removed, these striatal neurons fire more, the GPe is suppressed, and the released subthalamic nucleus drives the GPi harder. Both changes increase GPi inhibition of the VA and VL thalamus, so motor cortex receives less excitation and movements are hard to start and scale (bradykinesia).

blocks.predict: Early Huntington disease causes chorea, yet late Huntington disease often causes rigidity and slowness. Why does the movement disorder change?
blocks.explain: The indirect pathway neurons die first, lowering GPi output and releasing the thalamus. Later, direct pathway neurons die too, the go signal fails, and the picture becomes hypokinetic.
blocks.check: The two pathways and the table of disorders by mechanism.

sections.title: Cerebellar coordination and vermis versus hemisphere lesions

blocks.text: The cerebellum does not start movements, and losing it does not cause weakness. It compares the movement the cortex intended with the movement that is actually happening and corrects its direction, force, range, and timing. Mossy fibers bring a copy of the motor command from the pontine nuclei through the middle cerebellar peduncle, and feedback from muscles, joints, and the vestibular system through the spinocerebellar tracts and vestibular nuclei. Climbing fibers from the contralateral inferior olive enter through the inferior peduncle and signal errors that drive motor learning.

All of this converges on Purkinje cells, the only output of the cerebellar cortex. Purkinje cells are GABAergic and inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial) and the lateral vestibular nucleus. The deep nuclei send the cerebellum's mainly excitatory output, mostly through the superior cerebellar peduncle. The cerebellar cortex therefore works by sculpting the activity of the deep nuclei rather than by driving movement directly.

blocks.title: Functional zones of the cerebellum
rows: Fastigial nucleus to vestibulospinal and reticulospinal systems
Posture and axial muscles of both sides
Truncal ataxia, wide-based gait, both sides affected
Dentate nucleus to VL thalamus and motor cortex
Planning and timing of skilled limb movement
blocks.caption: Midline structures control the trunk on both sides; lateral structures control the limbs on the same side.

blocks.text: The vermis works with the medial descending systems that control axial muscles on both sides of the body. A vermis lesion therefore causes truncal ataxia: an unsteady trunk, a wide-based staggering gait, and difficulty standing or sitting without support, while the arms may test nearly normal. The unsteadiness is present with the eyes open, because it is a failure of coordination rather than of sensory input. Chronic alcohol use degenerates the anterior superior vermis and produces this pattern of gait ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination.

Each hemisphere works with the lateral corticospinal system that controls the limbs, so a hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral limb ataxia. The patient overshoots or undershoots a target (dysmetria), shows a tremor that grows as the finger nears the target (intention tremor, absent at rest, unlike the resting tremor of Parkinson disease), cannot perform rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia), has reduced tone, and tends to veer or fall toward the side of the lesion. Speech may become slurred and irregular in rhythm (scanning dysarthria). The signs are ipsilateral because the path is crossed twice, as shown below.

blocks.title: Why cerebellar hemisphere signs are ipsilateral
steps: Hemisphere Purkinje cells shape dentate nucleus output
Dentate fibers leave in the superior cerebellar peduncle
First crossing in the midbrain
Contralateral VL thalamus to contralateral motor cortex
Second crossing: corticospinal tract decussates in the medulla
Corrections act on limbs on the side of the lesion
blocks.caption: Two decussations cancel, so a right hemisphere lesion disturbs the right limbs.

blocks.predict: A patient with a cerebellar hemisphere tumor and a patient with dorsal column degeneration both sway when standing. Which one gets markedly worse when the eyes close?
blocks.explain: The patient with dorsal column disease. Vision substitutes for lost proprioception, so removing it unmasks the deficit (a positive Romberg sign). The cerebellar patient is unsteady with eyes open as well, because the problem is the coordination of movement, not the sensory input.

sections.title: Thalamic relay nuclei, thalamic infarction, and thalamic pain syndrome

blocks.text: The thalamus is the paired gray mass of the diencephalon on either side of the third ventricle. Nearly every pathway that reaches the cerebral cortex synapses here first; smell is the main exception, reaching olfactory cortex directly. The specific relay nuclei each receive one kind of input and project to one cortical area, and that area sends dense fibers back to the same nucleus to regulate the relay. The thalamus is therefore an active gate, not a simple wire, and a lesion of a relay nucleus produces nearly the same deficit as a lesion of its cortical target.

blocks.title: Thalamic relay nuclei
rows: Medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract: contralateral body touch, position, pain, temperature
Trigeminothalamic fibers (contralateral face) and taste from the solitary nucleus
Somatosensory cortex face area; gustatory cortex (insula and frontal operculum)
Primary visual cortex through the optic radiations
Dentate nucleus of the cerebellum and GPi of the basal ganglia
blocks.caption: Lateral geniculate for vision and medial geniculate for hearing; VPL for the body and VPM for the face and taste.

blocks.text: Other nuclei serve memory, emotion, and arousal rather than relay: the anterior nucleus belongs to the limbic circuit, the mediodorsal nucleus connects with prefrontal cortex and is damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, and the intralaminar nuclei carry arousal signals to the cortex (C06). Projections from VPL and VPM pass through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, which lies immediately lateral to the thalamus.

The ventral posterior nuclei are supplied mainly by thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery, small penetrating vessels that are prone to lacunar infarction in chronic hypertension. Because VPL and VPM together receive every somatic modality from the opposite side, an infarct confined to them causes contralateral loss of touch, position, pain, and temperature over the face, arm, and leg, without weakness (pure sensory stroke). A larger lesion that reaches the internal capsule adds contralateral hemiparesis.

Weeks to months after such an infarct, as sensation partly returns, some patients develop thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome): constant burning or aching pain on the numb side, with light touch or cold felt as pain (allodynia) and an exaggerated, delayed response to painful stimuli (hyperpathia). This is central neuropathic pain. It is thought to arise because deafferented thalamic and cortical neurons become hyperexcitable and the inhibitory influence that normal sensory input exerts on pain processing is lost.

sections.title: Brainstem levels of the cranial nerve nuclei and the regions of the spinal cord

blocks.text: Cranial nerve nuclei are arranged roughly in numerical order down the brainstem, so the nerves involved in a lesion give its level. The midbrain holds the oculomotor (III) and Edinger-Westphal nuclei at the level of the superior colliculus and the trochlear (IV) nucleus at the level of the inferior colliculus. The pons holds the trigeminal (V) main sensory and motor nuclei, the abducens (VI) and facial (VII) motor nuclei in its lower part, and the vestibular and cochlear (VIII) nuclei at the pontomedullary junction. The medulla holds the nuclei of the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and hypoglossal (XII) nerves. The trigeminal sensory nuclei, however, extend from the midbrain into the upper cervical cord, where the spinal accessory (XI) nucleus also lies.

blocks.title: Cranial nerve nuclei by brainstem level
rows: III and Edinger-Westphal (superior colliculus level); IV (inferior colliculus level)
V (main sensory, motor); VI and VII (lower pons); VIII (pontomedullary junction)
Jaw, lateral gaze, facial, and hearing or vestibular signs
IX, X (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor nucleus of X, solitary nucleus); XII
Swallowing, voice, gag, and tongue signs
XI (spinal accessory); spinal trigeminal nucleus continues here
Weak shoulder shrug and head turning
blocks.caption: The somatic motor nuclei for the eye and tongue muscles (III, IV, VI, XII) lie near the midline, so medial brainstem lesions tend to involve them.

blocks.text: Brainstem lesions classically produce crossed signs: an ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy, because cranial motor neurons and their exiting fibers do not cross (the trochlear nerve is the exception, crossing before it exits), with contralateral hemiparesis, because the corticospinal tract has not yet crossed. The cranial nerve gives the level; long tract signs place the lesion inside the brainstem.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing a crossed brainstem lesion
blocks.text: Right upper motor neuron hemiparesis, right loss of position and vibration sense, and a tongue deviating to the left. The tongue points toward the weak side, so left XII is affected, placing the lesion in the medulla. Right hemiparesis means the left pyramid is damaged above its decussation; right proprioceptive loss means the left medial lemniscus, already crossed, is involved. All three lie in the left medial medulla, supplied by the anterior spinal or vertebral artery.

In the spinal cord, central gray matter is shaped like an H. The dorsal horn receives sensory input, the ventral horn contains alpha and gamma motor neurons, and from T1 to L2 a lateral horn holds sympathetic preganglionic neurons; sacral parasympathetic neurons at S2 to S4 sit in the intermediate gray without forming a distinct horn. The gray matter swells into the cervical (about C4 to T1) and lumbosacral (about L2 to S3) enlargements, which supply the limbs through the brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.

blocks.title: Spinal cord white columns
cols: Side of deficit below a cord lesion
rows: Fasciculus gracilis (legs, medial) and cuneatus (arms, above about T6)
Contralateral (crosses within one to two segments)
blocks.caption: Where each tract crosses determines which side loses function below a one-sided cord lesion.

blocks.text: The vertebral column grows longer than the cord during fetal life and childhood, so the cord ends as the conus medullaris near the L1 to L2 vertebral level in adults (lower, near L3, at birth). Below it, lumbar and sacral roots descend in the dural sac as the cauda equina. The dural sac continues to about S2, which is why a needle introduced at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5 reaches cerebrospinal fluid among mobile roots without striking the cord. For the same reason, cord segments lie progressively higher than their numbered vertebrae.

sections.title: The ascending reticular activating system, coma, delirium, and brain death

blocks.text: Consciousness has two components. Arousal, the level of wakefulness, depends on the brainstem; awareness, the content of experience, depends on the cerebral hemispheres. Arousal is maintained by the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS), a group of neurons in the tegmentum of the upper pons and midbrain. They include cholinergic neurons of the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus, and serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei. Their projections reach the cortex through the intralaminar and other thalamic nuclei and, by a second route, through the hypothalamus and basal forebrain, which add histamine, orexin, and acetylcholine.

blocks.title: How the brainstem keeps the cortex awake
steps: Reticular neurons in upper pons and midbrain fire tonically
Acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and serotonin are released rostrally
Thalamic relay and intralaminar nuclei shift to tonic firing
Hypothalamus and basal forebrain add direct cortical activation
Both hemispheres are depolarized and responsive
Arousal is maintained
blocks.caption: Coma follows interruption of this system at its brainstem origin or failure of both hemispheres it activates.

blocks.text: Coma is unarousable unresponsiveness with the eyes closed. It requires one of two things: damage to the ARAS in the upper pons, midbrain, or thalamus, or dysfunction of both hemispheres. Diffuse causes include hypoxia, hypoglycemia, liver or kidney failure, drug intoxication, and seizures. A large lesion of one hemisphere does not cause coma by itself; it does so when swelling shifts the brain and compresses the midbrain, as in transtentorial herniation, often heralded by an ipsilateral dilated pupil from compression of CN III. Lesions below the upper pons spare arousal, which is why a ventral pontine infarct can leave a patient fully awake but unable to move anything except the eyes vertically and the eyelids (locked-in syndrome).

Delirium is different. It is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, often with disorganized thinking and a changing level of alertness, caused by a systemic insult such as infection, medication, alcohol withdrawal, or metabolic derangement. The patient can be roused, the course fluctuates over hours, the EEG shows diffuse slowing, and the state usually clears when the cause is corrected.

Brain death is the irreversible loss of all function of the entire brain, including the brainstem. It is declared only when the cause is known and confounders such as sedative drugs, hypothermia, and severe metabolic disturbance have been excluded. The findings are coma, absence of every brainstem reflex (pupillary light, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, gag, and cough), and apnea: no breathing effort even when arterial PCO2 rises to at least about 60 mmHg, a level that would strongly drive an intact medullary respiratory center. Spinal reflexes can persist because the cord is not part of the brain.

blocks.title: Disorders of consciousness
rows: Eyes open, sleep and wake cycles
Vertical eye movement and blinking preserved
blocks.caption: Arousal tracks the brainstem and awareness tracks the hemispheres.

blocks.predict: A patient after a basilar artery occlusion lies motionless, but blinks on command and looks up when asked. Is this patient in coma?
blocks.explain: No. The infarct lies in the ventral pons, interrupting corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers below the ARAS, so arousal and awareness are intact. This is locked-in syndrome, and it must not be mistaken for coma or brain death.
blocks.check: The location of the ARAS and the table of disorders of consciousness.

integration.text: Localization is the common thread of this chapter. Anatomy supplies the map: which side a pathway crosses, which artery feeds a region, and where cranial nerve nuclei sit. Physiology explains the deficit: the basal ganglia gate movement through disinhibition, the cerebellum compares intention with performance, the thalamus relays and filters, and the brainstem keeps the cortex aroused. Pathology names the processes that remove each structure: lacunar infarcts in the thalamus and internal capsule, Lewy body degeneration of the nigra, polyglutamine toxicity in the caudate, alcohol injury to the vermis, and herniation that compresses the midbrain.

The rules have limits. Language dominance is not universal, cortical maps are larger for some body parts in some people, and real infarcts rarely respect a single nucleus, so mixed pictures are common. Reasoning from what each structure contributes and where its pathways cross is more reliable than memorizing syndromes.

summary: Primary motor and sensory strips are somatotopic: leg medial (ACA), face and arm lateral (MCA), with contralateral deficits.
Calcarine cortex lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often macular sparing; one-sided auditory cortex lesions barely reduce hearing.
Broca aphasia is nonfluent with comprehension intact; Wernicke aphasia is fluent with comprehension poor; both impair repetition.
The GPi tonically inhibits the motor thalamus; the direct pathway releases this brake and the indirect pathway, through the subthalamic nucleus, tightens it.
Dopamine excites D1 direct neurons and inhibits D2 indirect neurons, so both actions favor movement; losing it in Parkinson disease raises GPi output.
Early Huntington disease removes indirect pathway neurons, lowers GPi output, and causes chorea; a subthalamic infarct causes contralateral hemiballismus.
Vermis lesions cause bilateral truncal ataxia and a wide-based gait; hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia because of a double decussation.

VPL relays the body, VPM the face and taste, LGN vision, MGN hearing, and VL cerebellar and basal ganglia output; a VPL and VPM infarct gives contralateral sensory loss and may later cause thalamic pain.
Cranial nerve nuclei descend in order (III and IV midbrain, V to VIII pons, IX, X, XII medulla); crossed signs place a lesion in the brainstem; the adult conus ends near L1 to L2.
Coma needs upper brainstem ARAS damage or bilateral hemisphere failure; delirium fluctuates and is reversible; brain death is irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem function with apnea.

verify: Brodmann area numbers for Broca (44, 45) and Wernicke (posterior 22) areas are standard, but some texts include area 39 or 40 in Wernicke area; confirm what NABNE expects.
Left hemisphere language dominance is quoted as about 95% in right-handed people and about 60% to 70% in left-handed people; figures vary by source.
The degree of nigral neuron loss before Parkinson signs appear is quoted from about 50% to 80%; this chapter says most neurons without a number.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponym Dejerine-Roussy syndrome and the name medial medullary syndrome, or only descriptive terms.

Adult conus level is quoted as L1 to L2 with a normal range of about T12 to L3; the newborn level is quoted as about L3 (some texts give L2 to L3). The lower limit of the dural sac (about S2) also varies slightly by source.

Segment ranges of the cervical (stated here as about C4 to T1; some texts give C5 to T1) and lumbosacral (stated here as about L2 to S3; some texts give L1 to S2) enlargements differ between anatomy texts.

Brain death criteria follow the current US consensus (2023 adult and pediatric guideline): apnea threshold PaCO2 of at least 60 mmHg and at least 20 mmHg above baseline, and core temperature at least about 36 °C (96.8 °F) before testing; confirm the version NABNE uses.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: basal-ganglia-circuit (direct and indirect pathways with excitatory and inhibitory links), brainstem-cn-levels (dorsal view of cranial nerve nuclei by level), and spinal-cord-cross-section (horns and white columns with tract positions).
